extracted.intended_audience: PolitiFact readers, editors, and journalists interested in fact-checking standards
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures used by PolitiFact to select, research, and rate the accuracy of political claims (Truth-O-Meter and Flip-O-Meter), including sourcing, editorial review, and corrections policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of claims to check (who is checked)
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact checks claims by elected officials, candidates, leaders of political parties and political activists. We examine officials at all levels of government, from county commissioners to U.S. senators, from city council members to the president. We also check claims by groups involved in the discourse -- political parties, advocacy groups and political action committees. We check claims by pundits, talk show hosts and columnists. We also examine claims in widely circulated chain e-mails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state sites follow the same principles as the national site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources and transparency requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: PolitiFact relies on on-the-record interviews and publishes a list of sources with every Truth-O-Meter item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, the list includes links to sources that are freely available, although some sources rely on paid subscriptions. The goal is to help readers judge for themselves whether they agree with the ruling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim selection — verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the statement rooted in a fact that is verifiable? We don’t check opinions, and we recognize that in the world of speechmaking and political rhetoric, there is license for hyperbole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every day, PolitiFact staffers look for statements that can be checked. We comb through speeches, news stories, press releases, campaign brochures, TV ads, Facebook postings and transcripts of TV and radio interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim selection — potential to mislead (impression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the statement leaving a particular impression that may be misleading?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We select the most newsworthy and significant ones because we can't check all claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim selection — significance (avoid minor 'gotchas')
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the statement significant? We avoid minor "gotchas" on claims that obviously represent a slip of the tongue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because we can't possibly check all claims, we select the most newsworthy and significant ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim selection — likelihood to be propagated
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the statement likely to be passed on and repeated by others?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We prioritize claims that are likely to spread or influence public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim selection — public curiosity test
rubrics_metrics.description: Would a typical person hear or read the statement and wonder: Is that true?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staffers use this question to gauge whether a claim merits checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-O-Meter goal
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal of the Truth-O-Meter is to reflect the relative accuracy of a statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: TRUE
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement is accurate and there’s nothing significant missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highest level of accuracy on the six-point scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: MOSTLY TRUE
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement is accurate but needs clarification or additional information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when the core claim is true but important context or nuance is missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: HALF TRUE
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement is partially accurate but leaves out important details or takes things out of context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to claims mixing accurate and inaccurate elements or where omission alters meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: MOSTLY FALSE
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement contains an element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: FALSE
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement is not accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: PANTS ON FIRE
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement is not accurate and makes a ridiculous claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for the most egregious, demonstrably false assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words matter
rubrics_metrics.description: We pay close attention to the specific wording of a claim. Is it a precise statement? Does it contain mitigating words or phrases?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for qualifiers and exact phrasing because small differences can change a ruling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context matters
rubrics_metrics.description: We examine the claim in the full context, the comments made before and after it, the question that prompted it, and the point the person was trying to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider surrounding remarks and the situation in which the statement was made to judge accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: People who make factual claims are accountable for their words and should be able to provide evidence to back them up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We will try to verify their statements, but we believe the burden of proof is on the person making the statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound statements handling ('Statements can be right and wrong')
rubrics_metrics.description: We sometimes rate compound statements that contain two or more factual assertions. In these cases, we rate the overall accuracy after looking at the individual pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess each assertion and then determine the appropriate overall rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of ruling
rubrics_metrics.description: Our rulings are based on when a statement was made and on the information available at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge a past statement by facts that became known later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-O-Meter editorial process
rubrics_metrics.description: A PolitiFact writer researches the claim and writes the Truth-O-Meter article with a recommended ruling. After the article is edited, it is reviewed by a panel of at least three editors that determines the Truth-O-Meter ruling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruling is a group editorial decision, not a sole reporter's unilateral rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flip-O-Meter purpose and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The Flip-O-Meter rates an official's consistency on an issue. The rating is not making a value judgment about a politician who changes positions on an issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is an analysis of a shift and rates the amount of change; voters may value flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flip-O-Meter ratings (No Flip / Half Flip / Full Flop)
rubrics_metrics.description: No Flip – No significant change in position. Half Flip – A partial change in position. Full Flop – A complete change in position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writing, editing and rating process for Flip-O-Meter items is the same as the process for Truth-O-Meter items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise meters (Obameter, GOP Pledge-O-Meter etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Promise meters rate the status of elected officials' campaign promises (e.g., the Obameter and the GOP Pledge-O-Meter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These track the status of promises rather than single factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections and updates policy
rubrics_metrics.description: When we make a mistake, we correct it and note it on the original item. In the case of a factual error, an editor's note will be added and labeled 'CORRECTION' explaining how the article has been changed. In the case of clarifications or updates, an editor's note will be added and labeled 'UPDATE' explaining how the article has been changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the mistake is significant, we will reconvene the three-editor panel. If there is a new ruling, we will rewrite the item and put the correction at the top indicating how it's been changed. Readers who see an error should contact the writer or editor; names and contact links are listed on every Truth-O-Meter item.
